claims.text: Some refractory BCC high-entropy alloys possess unexpectedly high strength at elevated temperatures.
The elevated-temperature strength and strength retention of NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV alloys are predominantly controlled by edge dislocations.
The thermoelastic stability of refractory BCC high-entropy alloys is predominantly controlled by edge dislocations.
Plastic flow in conventional elemental BCC metals and dilute BCC alloys is generally controlled by screw dislocations.
NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV are examples of refractory BCC high-entropy alloys relevant to the hypothesis.
As-cast or stress-relieved specimens have a typical baseline distribution of dislocations suitable for this comparison.
Cold working followed by partial annealing can selectively tailor the edge-dislocation density while maintaining otherwise comparable samples.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 600 degrees Celsius and well below the alloy melting point under quasi-static loading.
Edge dislocations interact with local stress fields produced by random alloy constituents.
Interactions between edge dislocations and local alloy stress fields impede dislocation motion.
A higher density of edge dislocations increases dislocation interactions and pinning.
Increased interaction and pinning reduce dislocation mobility at high temperature.
Reduced edge-dislocation mobility enhances high-temperature yield strength.
Reduced edge-dislocation mobility reduces thermoelastic softening.
Samples with a higher controlled edge-dislocation density will have higher yield strength than baseline samples.
Samples with a higher controlled edge-dislocation density will exhibit less thermoelastic softening than baseline samples.
The hypothesis is limited to refractory BCC high-entropy alloys similar to NbTaTiV or CrMoNbV in regimes dominated by dislocation-mediated plasticity.
In-situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution TEM can be combined to investigate dislocation structures during deformation in these alloys.
